items.title: Banksy's self-shredding
items.claim: In October 2018 a Banksy work partially shredded during a Sotheby's auction. What happened to the price after the stunt?

options.text: It sold for the auction price, then resold in 2021 for around £18.6 million
The buyer sued and won damages

items.reveal:
Originally hammered at around £1 million on 5 October 2018, the partially shredded work was renamed Love Is in the Bin and resold in October 2021 for around £18.6 million.

The shredder was concealed in the frame.
items.why: Critiques of art markets can become market assets themselves.

items.title: What happened to the original Fountain
items.claim: Marcel Duchamp submitted Fountain, a signed urinal, to the Society of Independent Artists in New York in 1917. What is true about the original object today?

options.text: It is in the Met's permanent collection
It was lost; existing versions are 1960s replicas authorised by Duchamp
It is on permanent display at MoMA
It was destroyed at the original exhibition

items.reveal_title: The original was lost; all 'Fountains' are later replicas
items.reveal:
The Society of Independent Artists never displayed it; the original disappeared. From the 1960s Duchamp authorised replicas, now in collections including the Tate and Centre Pompidou.

A 2004 survey of 500 art-world figures voted Fountain the most influential artwork of the 20th century.
items.why: Conceptual art's value can attach to the idea, not the original object.

items.title: Warhol's first soup cans
items.claim: Andy Warhol's first Campbell's Soup Cans exhibition was in which city in 1962?
items.reveal:
The 32 canvases (one per Campbell's variety) were priced at around $100 each. Ferus's owner Irving Blum bought the entire series for around $1,000 and later sold it to MoMA for around $15 million.

The work consolidated Pop Art's place in American museums within a decade.
items.why: Pop Art's commercial trajectory mirrored the consumer culture it depicted.
